intro: Eight cases that get harder as you go: benign tumors (vestibular schwannoma, meningioma), brain metastases, gliomas, and spinal cord compression. Each starts with a one-liner, then gives you more information step by step: the MRI and pathology, the diagnosis or grade, the treatment, the dose and targets, the landmark trials, and the side effects and follow-up. Some steps are multiple choice, some are fill-in-the-blank.

cases.title: Case 1: Ringing in One Ear
cases.oneLiner: A 49-year-old man has a year of gradual hearing loss and ringing in his right ear. His audiogram shows asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss on the right.

steps.label: Workup
steps.prompt: What is the best test for asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss?
choices: MRI of the internal auditory canals with contrast
steps.explanation: One-sided sensorineural hearing loss or tinnitus needs a contrast MRI of the internal auditory canals to look for a vestibular schwannoma.

steps.label: Origin
steps.caption: Axial T1 post-contrast MRI: right vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle (patient's right on your left). Hellerhoff, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.
steps.prompt: MRI shows a 1.6 cm enhancing mass widening the right internal auditory canal and extending into the cerebellopontine angle. Which nerve does it arise from?
steps.explanation: Vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) arise from the Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve. The 'ice cream cone' shape comes from the canal portion plus the CPA portion. Hearing loss is from pressure on the neighboring cochlear nerve.

steps.label: Grade
steps.prompt: It grew 3 mm in a year, touches the brainstem, but doesn't compress it. What is the Koos grade?
steps.explanation: Koos I is in the canal only, II reaches into the CPA, III fills the CPA and touches the brainstem, and IV compresses the brainstem.

steps.label: Treatment
steps.prompt: He wants to avoid surgery and his hearing is still serviceable. What is the best option?
steps.explanation: For a growing small-to-medium schwannoma, SRS offers high tumor control without an operation. Surgery remains important for large Koos IV tumors with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus, and for selected patients.

steps.label: Dose
steps.prompt: Give the SRS dose and the key hearing constraint.
steps.answer: 12-13 Gy to the tumor margin, keeping the cochlea mean dose at about 4 Gy or less.
steps.explanation: Facial nerve injury is rare at these doses. Hearing still tends to decline slowly over years.

steps.label: Nine months later
steps.prompt: Nine months after SRS, MRI shows the tumor is slightly larger with a darker center. He feels fine. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Pseudoprogression: temporary swelling that is expected at about 6-18 months after SRS
steps.explanation: Transient enlargement with central loss of enhancement is common after SRS for schwannomas and usually settles. Keep watching with serial MRI before calling it failure.

cases.title: Case 2: Double Vision
cases.oneLiner: A 55-year-old woman has 6 months of double vision when she looks to the left.

steps.label: Diagnosis
steps.caption: Coronal T1 post-contrast MRI of a different meningioma: a homogeneously enhancing parasagittal mass. James Heilman, MD, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
steps.prompt: MRI shows a 2.5 cm homogeneously enhancing mass in the left cavernous sinus with a dural tail, 4 mm from the optic chiasm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.explanation: A homogeneously enhancing, dura-based mass with a dural tail is a meningioma until proven otherwise; many are diagnosed on imaging without a biopsy. Her diplopia is from cranial nerve VI (or III/IV) in the cavernous sinus.

steps.label: Surgery?
steps.prompt: It grew from 2.0 to 2.5 cm over 18 months and encases the cavernous carotid. Why not simply remove it?
choices: Cavernous sinus tumors encase the carotid and cranial nerves, so resection risks stroke and new nerve deficits and is usually incomplete
steps.explanation: Accessible, symptomatic meningiomas go to surgery. Inaccessible ones, like this, are treated with radiation.

steps.label: Options
steps.prompt: Which radiation approaches fit a growing cavernous sinus meningioma?
choices: SRS 12-14 Gy, or fractionated RT 50.4-54 Gy
steps.explanation: Both give about 90-95% control at 5 years. The choice depends on size and distance from the optic apparatus.

steps.label: Choice
steps.prompt: With only 4 mm to the chiasm, which do you prefer, and why?
steps.answer: Fractionated RT (for example 50.4-54 Gy in 28-30 fractions) or hypofractionated SRT, because single-fraction SRS may not keep the chiasm at 8-10 Gy or less.
steps.explanation: SRS works best when the tumor is a few millimeters away from the optic nerves and chiasm.

steps.label: Side effects
steps.prompt: What side effects will you counsel her about?
steps.answer: Fatigue, hair thinning where the beams enter, headache, and rarely injury to nearby nerves (vision loss from optic nerve or chiasm injury) or the pituitary (hormone deficiency over years).
steps.explanation: Her double vision may improve, stay the same, or rarely worsen; tumor control means stopping growth, not making it disappear.

cases.title: Case 3: New Headaches
cases.oneLiner: A 58-year-old woman with EGFR-negative lung adenocarcinoma, controlled in the chest on chemo-immunotherapy, has two weeks of new headaches.

steps.label: Approach
steps.prompt: Thin-slice MRI shows three enhancing lesions: 1.5 cm, 1.2 cm, and 2.6 cm, with mild edema. KPS 90. What is the best approach?
steps.explanation: SRS alone is preferred for limited, safely treatable brain metastases. Lesion number matters, but so do total volume, size, location, symptoms, and prognosis; she is symptomatic, so treatment shouldn't be delayed. Surgery is for a large lesion, major mass effect, or when tissue is needed.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Why not add whole-brain RT to the SRS? Which trial showed more cognitive decline with no survival gain?
steps.explanation: N0574: adding WBRT improved intracranial control but caused more cognitive decline and did not improve survival.

steps.label: Prognosis
steps.prompt: Estimate her GPA (2008): age 58, KPS 90, 3 metastases, extracranial disease present.
steps.explanation: The GPA helps match treatment intensity to prognosis.

steps.label: Doses
steps.caption: SRS plan for a resection cavity and an intact metastasis: prescription isodose in green, low-dose spill in blue. Lewis J et al., Cureus 2025 (PMC12414254), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: What single-fraction doses for the 2.6 cm lesion and the two smaller ones?
steps.answer: 18 Gy for the 2.6 cm lesion; 24 Gy for each lesion 2 cm or smaller.
steps.explanation: RTOG 90-05: 2 cm or less 24 Gy, 2-3 cm 18 Gy, 3-4 cm 15 Gy. Larger lesions or cavities use 27 Gy in 3 or 30 Gy in 5.

steps.label: Follow-up
steps.prompt: What follow-up does she need after SRS alone?
steps.answer: MRI every 2-3 months, with SRS for any new lesions.
steps.explanation: Radionecrosis (about 5-10%) is the main late risk, higher with larger lesions and with immunotherapy.

steps.label: What if
steps.caption: Hippocampal-avoidance whole-brain plan: the two cool spots in the middle are the spared hippocampi. Yang X et al., Eur J Med Res 2023 (PMC9841677), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: Change one detail: the MRI shows 15 metastases and her systemic disease is controlled. Which approach protects memory best if you treat the whole brain?
choices: SRS to the largest lesion only
steps.explanation: NRG CC001: HA-WBRT plus memantine caused less cognitive failure than WBRT plus memantine.

cases.title: Case 4: Lost Words
cases.oneLiner: A 61-year-old man has a new seizure and 3 weeks of trouble finding words and headaches.

steps.label: Next step
steps.caption: Axial T1 post-contrast MRI: left temporal mass with a thick, irregular enhancing rim around a necrotic center. Armed Forces Institute of Pathology, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.
steps.prompt: MRI shows a 4 cm left temporal mass with thick, irregular ring enhancement around a necrotic center and surrounding FLAIR signal. What is the best next step?
steps.explanation: For a presumed high-grade glioma, maximal safe resection gives the diagnosis and molecular markers, relieves mass effect, and improves survival. Near language areas, awake mapping helps. Start dexamethasone and an antiseizure drug.

steps.label: Diagnosis
steps.context: Post-op MRI (48 h): gross total resection of the enhancing tumor. Pathology: IDH-wildtype glioma with necrosis and microvascular proliferation; MGMT promoter methylated. KPS 90.
steps.prompt: What is the integrated WHO 2021 diagnosis?
steps.answer: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4 (MGMT promoter methylated)
steps.explanation: An IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumor with necrosis and/or microvascular proliferation meets criteria for glioblastoma. MGMT methylation is prognostic and associated with greater benefit from temozolomide.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial established 60 Gy in 30 fractions with daily temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide?
steps.explanation: Stupp improved median survival (14.6 vs 12.1 months) and 5-year survival (about 10% vs 2%). EF-14 added tumor treating fields to adjuvant TMZ.

steps.label: Targets
steps.prompt: Describe the target volumes.
steps.answer: GTV = resection cavity plus any residual enhancement (± FLAIR); CTV = GTV + about 1.5-2 cm, trimmed at bone, falx, and tentorium; PTV + 3-5 mm. 60 Gy in 30 fractions (or FLAIR to 46 Gy, then a boost to 60 Gy).
steps.explanation: Respect the optic chiasm, optic nerves, and brainstem (about 54 Gy).

steps.label: Counseling
steps.prompt: What side effects do you counsel him on?
steps.answer: Fatigue, hair loss in the treated area, scalp irritation, headache or worsening symptoms from swelling (steroids), and temozolomide effects such as nausea, constipation, and low counts (low platelets in particular). Long term: memory and thinking changes.
steps.explanation: Patients on concurrent TMZ also get PCP prophylaxis because of lymphopenia.

steps.label: Eight months later
steps.caption: Treated glioblastoma with a new enhancing lesion (left) proven to be radiation necrosis; the perfusion map (right) shows it is not hyperperfused. Mohamedbaqer Easa A et al., Cureus 2025 (PMC12393895), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: Eight months after RT, MRI shows a new enhancing area in the treated region. Perfusion imaging is low. He feels well. What is most likely?
steps.explanation: Enhancement inside the high-dose field months after RT can be treatment effect. Low perfusion favors necrosis over tumor, which is usually hyperperfused. Short-interval follow-up, advanced imaging, or tissue sort it out.

cases.title: Case 5: She Lives Alone
cases.oneLiner: A 78-year-old woman with a biopsy-proven IDH-wildtype, MGMT-methylated glioblastoma in the left temporal lobe has a KPS of 60. She lives alone and wants to minimize trips to the hospital.

steps.label: Approach
steps.caption: Axial FLAIR MRI of a left temporal glioblastoma with extensive surrounding FLAIR signal and mass effect. Tiwari S, Gyawali I, Cureus 2024 (PMC10944577), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: Which approach is best supported by evidence for her?
steps.explanation: Shorter courses respect her goals and her frailty while keeping the benefit of TMZ.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial showed that adding TMZ to 40 Gy in 15 fractions improved survival in patients 65 and older, especially with MGMT methylation?
steps.explanation: Perry established short-course RT plus TMZ for older patients. Roa showed 25 Gy in 5 matched 40 Gy in 15 in older or frail patients.

steps.label: If frailer
steps.prompt: What is reasonable if she becomes too frail for chemoRT?
choices: 25 Gy in 5 fractions alone, or TMZ alone (because she is MGMT methylated)
steps.explanation: Very frail patients can get 25 Gy in 5 (Roa), TMZ alone if MGMT-methylated (Nordic, NOA-08), or supportive care.

steps.label: Late toxicity
steps.prompt: Which late toxicity is she at risk for with a left temporal target?
steps.answer: Memory and language decline (left temporal lobe and hippocampus), fatigue, and steroid side effects.
steps.explanation: Discuss goals of care alongside treatment.

steps.label: Steroids
steps.prompt: She is on dexamethasone for edema. Which steroid side effects should you watch for?
steps.answer: High blood sugar, insomnia and mood changes, weight gain, thrush, proximal muscle weakness, GI upset or ulcers, infections, and bone loss.
steps.explanation: Taper to the lowest dose that controls symptoms.

cases.title: Case 6: The First Seizure
cases.oneLiner: A 38-year-old man has his first seizure. MRI shows a 5 cm non-enhancing, FLAIR-bright left frontal mass, and CT shows calcification in it.

steps.label: Diagnosis
steps.caption: Axial FLAIR MRI of a non-enhancing low-grade glioma in the left frontal and insular region (another patient). Vail M et al., Cureus 2026 (PMC12947947), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: Which diagnosis fits best?
steps.explanation: A young adult with a seizure and a frontal, cortical, non-enhancing, calcified tumor is an oligodendroglioma until proven otherwise.

steps.label: Pathology
steps.context: Subtotal resection (residual non-enhancing tumor near the motor strip). Pathology: IDH-mutant, 1p/19q codeleted, WHO grade 2.
steps.prompt: What is the integrated diagnosis?
steps.explanation: IDH mutation plus 1p/19q codeletion defines oligodendroglioma. IDH-mutant without codeletion is astrocytoma.

steps.label: Options
steps.prompt: Name two reasonable next steps given his residual tumor.
steps.answer: Vorasidenib to delay RT and chemo, or RT 50.4-54 Gy followed by PCV; close MRI surveillance with either approach.
steps.explanation: Residual tumor makes him higher risk. Vorasidenib is for residual or recurrent non-enhancing grade 2 IDH-mutant tumors.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial showed that RT plus PCV nearly doubled median overall survival (13.3 vs 7.8 years) in high-risk grade 2 gliomas?
steps.explanation: RTOG 9802 is the RT plus PCV trial. INDIGO showed vorasidenib delayed progression (PFS about 28 vs 11 months); CATNON is the grade 3 non-codeleted astrocytoma trial.

steps.label: Dose
steps.prompt: If RT is given, what dose and chemo?
steps.answer: About 54 Gy in 30 fractions (50.4-54 Gy), followed by PCV (procarbazine, lomustine, vincristine).
steps.explanation: Grade 3 oligodendroglioma would get 59.4 Gy plus PCV.

steps.label: Survivorship
steps.prompt: Why do late effects matter more for him than for a GBM patient, and what can reduce them?
choices: He may live decades, so memory, fatigue, and endocrine effects matter; hippocampal sparing and protons are often considered
Late effects only happen in children
steps.explanation: Lower-grade glioma patients live years to decades, so the plan weighs long-term cognition and quality of life.

cases.title: Case 7: Vomiting and Unsteady
cases.oneLiner: A 64-year-old man with metastatic melanoma on immunotherapy has 4 days of vomiting, headache, and unsteadiness.

steps.label: Next step
steps.prompt: MRI shows a single 4 cm right cerebellar metastasis compressing the 4th ventricle, with early hydrocephalus. What is the next step?
steps.explanation: A large lesion with mass effect and hydrocephalus needs surgery to relieve pressure quickly. SRS alone is for smaller lesions without dangerous mass effect.

steps.label: Adjuvant
steps.prompt: Gross total resection leaves a 3.5 cm cavity, with no other brain lesions. What adjuvant treatment is standard?
steps.explanation: Cavity SRS lowers the local recurrence risk after resection while sparing cognition.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trials support cavity SRS: better local control than observation, and better cognition than whole-brain RT?
steps.explanation: Mahajan compared cavity SRS with observation; N107C compared it with WBRT.

steps.label: Regimen
steps.caption: Fractionated SRS plan for a resection cavity (24 Gy in 3 fractions) and a separate intact metastasis, in another patient: prescription isodose in green. Lewis J et al., Cureus 2025 (PMC12414254), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: Give a common regimen for a 3.5 cm cavity.
steps.answer: Fractionated SRT, for example 27 Gy in 3 or 30 Gy in 5 fractions, to the cavity plus 1-2 mm (including the surgical tract and adjacent dura).
steps.explanation: Large cavities are fractionated to lower the risk of radionecrosis.

steps.label: Risk
steps.prompt: Which part of his treatment raises the risk of radionecrosis with SRS?
choices: Checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy given around the time of SRS
steps.explanation: Immunotherapy and larger target volumes both raise the radionecrosis risk.

steps.label: Eight months later
steps.prompt: Eight months later he has new headaches and MRI shows growing enhancement with a lot of edema at the cavity edge. How do you approach it?
steps.answer: Consider radionecrosis vs recurrence: advanced imaging (perfusion MRI, PET) or tissue to tell them apart. Treat symptomatic necrosis with steroids, then bevacizumab or laser ablation if needed; recurrence may need surgery or re-irradiation.

cases.title: Case 8: Back Pain and Weak Legs
cases.oneLiner: A 67-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has 2 weeks of worsening mid-back pain and 1 day of leg weakness and trouble walking.

steps.label: First move
steps.prompt: What is the first thing to do?
choices: Give dexamethasone and get an urgent MRI of the whole spine
steps.explanation: New neurologic deficits with back pain in a cancer patient are cord compression until proven otherwise. Steroids now, and MRI of the whole spine because other levels are often involved.

steps.label: Grade
steps.caption: Sagittal T2 MRI of the thoracic spine in another patient: a pathologic fracture with epidural tumor compressing the cord. Kuah T et al., Cancers 2022 (PMC9265325), CC BY 4.0.
steps.prompt: MRI shows a T10 metastasis with epidural tumor compressing the cord and no CSF visible around it at that level. What is the Bilsky grade?
steps.explanation: Bilsky 3 is cord compression with no CSF visible around the cord; 2 is compression with some CSF remaining; 1 is epidural disease without cord deformity. 2-3 is high-grade compression.

steps.label: Plan
steps.prompt: He is medically fit, has one level of compression, and the spine is stable. What's the plan?
choices: Urgent surgical decompression (stabilization if needed), then postoperative RT, with steroids
steps.explanation: For fit patients with a single level of high-grade compression, surgery plus RT keeps more patients walking.

steps.label: Trial
steps.prompt: Which trial showed more patients kept or regained the ability to walk with surgery plus RT than with RT alone?
steps.explanation: Patchell is why fit patients with cord compression get a surgical consult.

steps.label: Regimens
steps.prompt: Give RT regimens used for cord compression.
steps.answer: 8 Gy in 1, 20 Gy in 5, or 30 Gy in 10 fractions (after surgery, often 20-30 Gy); SBRT (for example 24 Gy in 2) for selected radioresistant or oligometastatic disease.
steps.explanation: Choose by prognosis, histology, and whether surgery was done.

steps.label: Prognosis
steps.prompt: What is the strongest predictor of whether he walks after treatment?
choices: Whether he can walk before treatment
steps.explanation: Ambulatory status at the start of treatment is the strongest predictor, which is why cord compression is treated as an emergency.
